title: AI Design Tools for Non-Designers — Canva Magic Studio, Figma Make & Miro/Whimsical AI

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Design used to be the one part of "AI can help me communicate" that stayed out of reach — you could ask Claude or ChatGPT to write the words, but turning that into a polished deck, a wireframe, or a whiteboard diagram still meant learning design software or waiting on a designer. That gap closed fast between 2025 and 2026. Canva's April 2026 "Canva AI 2.0" overhaul, Figma's prompt-to-prototype tool Figma Make, and the AI-diagramming layers now built into Miro and Whimsical mean a non-designer can go from a plain-language description to an editable, professional-looking deliverable in minutes — not a flat image, but a real layered file you (or an actual designer later) can keep editing. This lesson walks through all three, then has you actually build something you'll keep.

## Canva AI 2.0 — Conversational Design, Magic Layers, and Canva Code

At Canva Create 2026 (April 15–16), Canva announced Canva AI 2.0, built around a new proprietary **Canva Design Model** — a foundation model Canva describes as purpose-built to understand the structure, hierarchy, and layering of real design work, rather than just generating a flat image. Three things matter most for a non-designer:

**Conversational design.** Instead of typing one prompt and getting one static result, you open the Canva AI panel (from the homepage or the button in the top-left of the editor) and describe an idea, a goal, or even a rough unfinished thought. Canva assembles a fully layered, editable design — with layout, hierarchy, and your brand kit already applied — and keeps the conversation open so you can keep refining it in real time, the same way you'd iterate with a human designer.

**Magic Layers.** Point Magic Layers at any flat design — including AI images generated in ChatGPT or Gemini, not just Canva's own output — and it reconstructs the image into separate, selectable, movable layers you can edit individually: swap the headline, change the offer, resize for a different platform, recolor a background. Magic Layers launched to explosive adoption (9 million uses within about a month), though as of mid-2026 it's still a public beta limited to the US, UK, Canada, and Australia.

**Canva Code 2.0** is one of six new "intelligent workflows" launched alongside conversational design (the others: connectors, scheduling, web research, brand intelligence, and Sheets AI). The connectors are worth calling out on their own — they plug Canva AI directly into Slack, Gmail, Google Drive, Google Calendar, Notion, Zoom, HubSpot, Microsoft, Atlassian, and Linear, so Canva can pull in real content from tools you already use instead of starting from nothing.

Access: Canva AI 2.0's core conversational features work from a free account (capped at 50 AI actions/month), but Magic Layers and the full Magic Studio suite generally require Canva Pro (about $14.99/month).

## Figma Make — Prompt-to-Prototype with a Real Path to Engineering

Figma Make is Figma's prompt-to-code workflow, sitting in the Figma product suite alongside Figma Design, FigJam, Figma Slides, and Dev Mode. You describe an app idea or screen in plain language, and Figma Make generates responsive layouts, interaction logic, and sample data as a working, clickable prototype — no code required to get there, even though code is what's actually generated underneath.

Two 2026 refinements make this more usable for a non-designer specifically:

**"Plan before building."** Rather than generating straight from your first prompt, Figma Make can first produce a structured, editable plan — the screens, flows, and components it intends to build — so you can correct its understanding of your idea before it spends effort generating the wrong thing.

**Attachments as context.** You can attach existing designs, images, PDFs, or short video/audio clips to a Figma Make prompt, and it uses them as grounding — useful if you already have a rough sketch, a competitor screenshot, or a brand style guide you want it to match.

**Getting to real engineering — Dev Mode.** This is where Figma Make stops being a toy. When your prototype needs to become real code a developer will actually ship, Dev Mode looks for a **Code Connect** mapping — a link between a Figma component and its real counterpart in your codebase — before generating handoff code, so the output matches your team's actual component library instead of inventing new markup. A useful 2026 data point from Figma's own reporting: Figma Make gets the general structure of a well-prompted request right 70–80% of the time — specific brand colors and fine styling details still usually need a human pass.

Access note: Full-seat Figma users can publish and share Make files; View/Collab/Dev-seat users can still create and try Make files in drafts, which is enough for the workshop below even without a paid design seat.

## Miro AI and Whimsical AI — Whiteboards and Mind Maps from a Sentence

Diagramming is the other design task non-designers regularly need and rarely enjoy doing by hand — a project flowchart, an org chart, a decision tree, a mind map for planning. Two tools now do most of the manual layout work for you.

**Miro AI.** From the "Create with AI" panel, choose the Sidekicks library, pick Formats > Diagram or Mindmap, describe what you want, and Miro generates an editable sketch directly on your board — flowcharts, ER diagrams, UML sequence and class diagrams, and mind maps are all supported, and you can keep expanding branches or connecting the result to other content on the same infinite canvas. A genuinely useful 2026 beta feature is **Digitize Diagram**: photograph or upload a hand-drawn sketch, and Miro AI converts it into a fully editable digital diagram. Miro's interface is even adaptive — the same AI button is labeled "Sidekicks" on AI-heavy boards and "Create with AI" on diagram-heavy ones. Free-tier accounts get only 10 AI credits total for the whole team, so a real evaluation usually needs at least the Starter plan (25 credits per member).

**Whimsical AI.** Whimsical takes the opposite design bet: fewer features, a faster path from a text prompt to a clean mind map or flowchart, with a minimalist interface that product teams tend to prefer for quick planning documents. Its free tier is worth understanding before you rely on it: the 100 free AI actions are a **lifetime cap, not a monthly allowance**, so it's easy to burn through them faster than expected. Whimsical Pro starts at $10/user/month.

**Picking between them:** Whimsical wins when you want the fastest path to a clean, shareable diagram and don't need a full collaborative workspace. Miro wins when the diagram is one artifact inside a larger workshop, retrospective, or brainstorm you're running with a team.

## What These Tools Are — and Aren't — Good For

None of these tools replace a professional designer or engineer for anything customer-facing at scale, brand-critical, or safety-critical. What they're genuinely good for: a non-designer producing a real, presentable first draft — a one-pager, a wireframe, a whiteboard — fast enough that the AI-assisted version becomes the actual starting point for feedback, instead of a rough sketch someone else has to redo from scratch. The most common failure mode isn't the AI generating something broken; it's a non-designer treating the AI's confident-looking first draft as finished when it still needs a review pass for brand accuracy, factual correctness in any text it generated, and — for Figma Make specifically — an actual engineer's review before anything it generates ships to production.

**Cross-tool interoperability is the emerging pattern.** Magic Layers explicitly working on images generated by ChatGPT or Gemini, and Figma Make's ability to import outside designs, sketches, and PDFs as context, both point the same direction: none of these products assume you live entirely inside their walled garden. The realistic 2026 workflow is a non-designer bouncing a project between two or three of these tools — generate a rough visual somewhere, make it editable in Canva, turn a concept into a clickable screen in Figma Make, map the underlying process in Whimsical or Miro.

**Treat every AI-generated design as a draft, not a deliverable.** A conversational Canva design can misread your brand guidelines; a Figma Make prototype nails the general structure only 70–80% of the time by Figma's own numbers; a Miro or Whimsical diagram can confidently draw a process flow that skips a real edge case. None of that is a reason to avoid these tools — it's a reason to always do a human review pass before something goes to a client, a manager, or (for Figma Make) into a codebase, exactly the same discipline covered for AI-generated code and text elsewhere in this course.

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Build a Real One-Page Project Pitch with Canva AI 2.0
sections.content:
You'll produce a real, keepable one-pager for something you're actually working on — not a throwaway demo.

**Step 1 — Go to canva.com and sign in** (a free account is enough for this workshop). Open the Canva AI panel from the homepage, or from the button in the top-left of the editor.

**Step 2 — Describe a real project in conversation.** Pick something genuinely yours — a work proposal, a personal side project, a class assignment, a community idea. Prompt something like: *"Create a one-page pitch for [your real project]: the problem, the solution, why now, and next steps."*

**Step 3 — Refine conversationally, not by starting over.** Ask for specific changes: "make the tone more urgent," "swap the layout to lead with the problem," "add a budget section." This is the point of conversational design — you're iterating, not regenerating from scratch each time.

**Step 4 — If you have a flat image related to this project** (an AI-generated image from ChatGPT or Gemini, or a phone photo of a whiteboard sketch), run it through Magic Layers (canva.com/magic-layers) and pull at least one element from it into your editable design.

**Step 5 — Export as a PDF and save it somewhere real** (your notes, your drive, an actual email draft to send). This should be a document you could genuinely hand to someone today.

**Step 6 — Write a 2-sentence note:** what would you change if your actual employer's or organization's brand kit (logo, colors, fonts) were loaded into this design instead of Canva's defaults?

**Outcome:** a real one-page pitch document for something you actually care about, plus first-hand experience with conversational design and Magic Layers.

sections.question: You generated a flyer image using ChatGPT's image tool, but it's a single flat picture — you can't select or edit individual elements like the headline or the price. Which Canva feature is specifically designed to solve this?
options: Magic Layers — it reconstructs any flat image, including ones generated outside Canva, into separate editable layers
sections.explanation: Magic Layers is built exactly for this situation: it takes a flat design — whether it came from Canva's own generator, ChatGPT, or Gemini — and reconstructs it into selectable, movable layers you can edit individually (swap the headline, change the price, recolor a background). Canva Code 2.0 is a different workflow (one of the six new intelligent workflows for building interactive content), the Sheets AI connector deals with spreadsheet data, and brand kit matching applies to designs generated inside Canva's own conversational flow, not to importing an external flat image.

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Prototype or Diagram: Figma Make vs. Whimsical/Miro AI
sections.content:
Choose one path below based on what would actually be useful to you right now. Both produce a real artifact you can keep using.

**Path A — Figma Make (build a clickable prototype):**

1. Go to figma.com and open Figma Make (the Make tab, or figma.com/make). A free/Dev/Collab seat is enough to create and try a draft.
2. Describe a real, simple screen in plain language — a signup screen, a landing page, or a settings screen for an idea you actually have. If Figma Make offers a "plan before building" step, review the plan it proposes before letting it generate.
3. If you have a reference — a rough sketch, a competitor's screenshot, a brand style guide — attach it to your prompt as context.
4. Generate the prototype and actually click through it as if you were a user.
5. Open Dev Mode and look at how it handles handoff — even if you're not a developer, notice whether it references a Code Connect mapping or generates fresh markup.

**Path B — Whimsical or Miro AI (build a real flowchart):**

1. Pick a real, recurring process from your work or life — an onboarding checklist, an approval workflow, a decision you make repeatedly.
2. In Whimsical (whimsical.com) or Miro ("Create with AI" > Sidekicks > Diagram/Mindmap), describe the process in one prompt.
3. Review the generated flowchart critically — add any step or branch it missed, since you know the real process better than the AI does.
4. If using Miro, try the Digitize Diagram beta: sketch a rough version by hand, photograph it, and upload it to see the AI convert it into an editable digital diagram.
5. Save or share the finished diagram somewhere you (or a colleague) would actually reference it again.

**Step 6 (either path) — Write a 2-sentence verdict:** how does this AI-generated first draft compare to what you'd have built manually, and roughly how much time do you think it saved you?

**Outcome:** a real clickable prototype or a real flowchart — something you'll actually use, not a one-off exercise.

sections.question: Your team plans to rely on Whimsical's free tier for ongoing diagramming at work. What's the most important thing to know about its AI action limit before committing to that plan?
options: The 100 free AI actions reset every month, so usage resets automatically
The 100 free AI actions are a lifetime cap, not a monthly allowance — a team can burn through them permanently much faster than expected
Free tier AI actions are unlimited but restricted to mind maps only
The free tier requires a credit card and auto-upgrades to Pro after 100 actions
sections.explanation: Whimsical's 100 free AI actions are a one-time, lifetime allowance for the account — not a monthly reset like many other freemium AI tools. A team that assumes it resets monthly (like Miro's credit system, which does allocate credits per plan period) can be surprised when AI generation stops working entirely partway through a project. If ongoing AI diagramming is part of your actual workflow, budget for Whimsical Pro ($10/user/month) rather than assuming the free tier will keep pace.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 2-19.** You now understand how Canva AI 2.0 (conversational design, Magic Layers, Canva Code 2.0), Figma Make (prompt-to-prototype, Plan before building, Dev Mode's Code Connect handoff), and Miro AI/Whimsical AI (Sidekicks diagram generation, Digitize Diagram) let a non-designer go from a plain-language description to an editable, real deliverable. You've built a real one-page project pitch in Canva and either a clickable prototype in Figma Make or a real flowchart in Whimsical/Miro — and you know why every AI-generated design still needs a human review pass before it ships.
